newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudis tread cautiously in moves towards Iran.
newsitem.headline: Saudis tread cautiously in moves towards Iran.

text.p: Saudi Arabia has responded favourably to Iranian overtures for better relations after years of strained ties and tension between the two oil giants.
But some in the kingdom remain wary of the Islamic republic.
A source familiar with official thinking in Riyadh said the Saudis had to deal cautiously with Iran, long accused of seeking to destabilise the strategic region.
The kingdom "must not sell itself short", the source said.
Moslem Shi'ite Iran, the Gulf's non-Arab power, has had tense relations with Sunni Saudi Arabia since the 1979 revolution in Iran.
Both countries have exchanged accusations and insults and diplomatic ties were severed after 402 people, mostly Iranians, died in riots during the 1987 pilgrimage to Mecca.
Relations were restored after the 1991 Gulf War, in which Iran remained neutral over Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Recent signs of a further improvement include a plan to restore direct air links later this year and a $15 million industrial cooperation deal with Iran's largest economic conglomerate.
The growing role in foreign affairs of King Fahd's designated heir, Crown Prince Abdullah, led to the latest Saudi move towards Iran, senior Gulf sources said on Sunday.
They said he got on well with Iran's outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and there had been several exchanges between the two men in recent months.
These included a chat on the sidelines of an Islamic summit in Pakistan in March which also touched on a June 1996 bomb attack in the kingdom that killed 19 U.S. airmen.
Crown Prince Abdullah had asked Rafsanjani, who leaves office next month, to visit the kingdom, the sources added.

Riyadh has yet to disclose the outcome of its investigation into the bombing. It has not publicly accused anyone of the attack, but Gulf diplomats say there have been hints of at least an indirect Iranian role.
Although hardliners in the Saudi royal family appear to have been consulted, some influential princes wanted to see concrete changes by Tehran before fully opening the door to it.
A Gulf source said Crown Prince Abdullah's effort came at a time when Washington appeared willing to reconsider its Iran containment policy if Tehran showed some flexibility.

"It is a big game involving many aspects like close Syrian ties with Iran, rapprochement with Iraq...and number two (Abdullah) is behind it," said the source. "He is trying to bring about some change to say (to Washington): 'Iran is willing to move in a new direction'."
To the surprise of many in the Gulf, Saudi Arabia sent Minister of State Abdul-Aziz bin Abdullah al-Khoweiter to Tehran in July with messages from King Fahd and the crown prince.
Gulf sources said the visit appeared to enjoy some backing from both hardline and moderate factions of the royal family as the envoy was a longtime close aide to King Fahd.
But a senior Arab diplomat in Riyadh doubted the attempt to improve ties had reached the extent of Riyadh's seeking to mediate between its Gulf neighbour Tehran and main ally Washington.
A Western diplomat said: "Expressing U.S. terms to Iran through Saudi or Kuwait is not the same as mediating."
He was referring to Washington's main demands for Tehran to abandon "terrorism", end objections to the Middle East peace process and stop efforts to buy and develop arms and nuclear capabilities.
Iran has repeatedly denied the charges.

The Los Angeles Times last week quoted a U.S. official as saying Riyadh had been a central intermediary in relaying the U.S. message to Tehran, adding that Washington "would like to end the estrangement".

But a source in Riyadh said "there are many unresolved issues" between Iran and Saudi Arabia "and mainly the Khobar bombing, which is still open", before the two could reach the point of fully normalising ties -- let alone Riyadh's moving to mediate on behalf of Washington.
But within the Saudi royal family Crown Prince Abdullah, a firm believer in Arab and Moslem solidarity, is expected to pursue a policy of "giving Iran a chance" over the next few months, he added.
"This does not mean that the others (hardline princes) are fully behind it or believe it will work, but rather that they agree to wait for the outcome," said a Gulf source.

Others in the region and some in the West appear to have decided to wait and see as Iran's newly elected President Mohammad Khatami takes office in August, amid hopes he might seek to ease suspicions by some neighbours.
